chunks: Components needed around a SoC. The question: When designing a system, what other components are needed in addition to a SoC?
A SoC ("What is a system on chip") cannot run alone.
It needs power at the right voltages, a clock to set its pace, a reset to start cleanly, and, for bigger chips, outside memory and storage.
It also needs connectors, interface chips and protection to reach the real world. The job is to list what the chip cannot make for itself, and why.
Think of a car engine sitting on a workbench. It is the heart of the car, but it goes nowhere without a fuel tank, a battery, a key to start it, and wheels. The SoC is the engine.
The supporting parts are the tank, key and wheels. A board with the chip but missing power or a clock does nothing.
The SoC is the hub. Arrows from the top row are things it cannot start without (power, clock, reset); double arrows below are interfaces to external devices.
Missing a top-row item means the board will not boot; missing a bottom-row item means the product lacks a feature.
Rail: a power line held at one fixed voltage, such as 0. 9 volts or 1. 8 volts. PMIC: one chip that makes several rails and switches them on in order.
Decoupling capacitor: a small capacitor beside a power pin that supplies quick bursts of current.
Crystal: a tiny part that vibrates at a precise frequency and gives the chip its clock beat. Reset: a signal that holds the chip in a known starting state until power is stable.
PHY: a chip that turns digital data into the signals a cable carries, such as Ethernet.
An application chip needs a 0. 9 volts core rail at 3 amps, fed from a 5 volts input. The core uses 0. 9 times 3 equals 2. 7 watts.
A regulator (a circuit that turns 5 volts into 0. 9 volts) that is 88% efficient draws 2. 7 over 0. 88 about 3. 07 watts from the input. That is about 3. 07 over 5 about 0.
61 amps at 5 volts. The board also needs more rails, a crystal, a reset circuit, memory, boot storage, and a PHY for Ethernet. That is the whole idea.
"Beyond the SoC you need power: a PMIC or regulators with the right rails, sequencing and decoupling, plus a charger if it's a battery product.
Clocks and reset: a crystal or oscillator, a 32 kilohertz RTC crystal and a reset supervisor. Memory: DRAM and boot flash or eMMC unless they're on-chip.
I/O parts: PHYs, connectors, ESD protection, level shifters and radios. Then sensors, display and user I/O, plus debug access, boot straps, test points and a thermal solution."
